## Where the Framing Breaks Down

### The Load Is Bounded and Not Known

**Everything in the power and thermal sections is an upper bound.** The article computes what the array
could generate and what the radiator could reject, and both are ceilings. The actual load could be a tenth
of either, and no public data distinguishes the cases.
**A bracket between 540 and 1,623 watts is a wide bracket** and the article should not be read as having
measured a kilowatt.

### The Drag Area Is Assumed

The ballistic coefficient of 623.75 kilograms per square metre rests on an assumed drag area of 8 square
metres and on the launch mass of 4,990 kilograms standing for the mass on orbit. **The drag area is not
published, and the mass on orbit is not either.** The makeup requirement in the drag
section is linear in the drag area, so nearly doubling the area roughly doubles every velocity increment, and
the qualitative conclusion survives that. **The altitude floor does not survive it unchanged**, and a reader
should treat 245.4 kilometres as an order rather than a number.

### The Propellant Load Is a Guess and It Propagates Widely

**The 500 kilogram propellant assumption appears in the altitude floor, in the aerobraking leverage ratio and in the plane change comparison**,
and no input in the article is less defensible. It was chosen as a round tenth of launch mass.
**Every ratio that divides by 310.6 metres per second should be read as scaling inversely with whatever the true load is.**
The aerobraking conclusion is robust to it, because a factor of 7.88 would survive a doubling of the
propellant load and still be decisive. The altitude floor is not robust to it.

### The Aerobraking Reconstruction Is Not a Reconstruction

The article computes what aerobraking could have done for a vehicle of this ballistic coefficient at various
perigees.
**It does not know what perigee was flown, how many passes were made, or what fraction of the apogee reduction was aerodynamic.**
The 100 kilometre figure is where the calendar closes, not where the vehicle went.

### The Solar Cycle Observation Is an Observation and Not a Finding About Intent

**A launch date is set by range availability, payload readiness, vehicle availability and policy**, and this
article has no evidence that the drag environment entered the decision. The arithmetic showing that the
record mission began in the quietest phase of the solar cycle is sound.
**Any inference from it about why the mission was flown when it was is not.**

### The Comparison With the Two Preceding Articles Is Neat and Should Be Distrusted for It

Three consecutive articles have found a demonstration tilted in a computable direction, in two directions.
**A pattern found three times in a series written by one author using one method is evidence about the method as much as about the aircraft.**
It is recorded here so that the closing article can test it against the vehicles that have not yet been
examined, rather than treated as established.

### The Article Assumes the Vehicle Is What It Appears to Be

**Every calculation here treats the X-37B as a five-tonne winged vehicle with a small array, a hypergolic propulsion system and a payload bay of published dimensions.**
If any of those is wrong, and a classified programme is entitled to have published a misleading
specification, then the calculations are internally consistent and externally worthless.
**There is no way to test that from outside**, and the article states it rather than assuming its way past
it.

## The Source Base

### The Vehicle's Own Cluster Is Thin, Which Is the Fifth Instance and the Fifth Reason

**Twenty research records in this survey carry the X-37 designation or the words orbital test vehicle in their titles.**
Twelve are space agency reports dated between 2000 and 2006. Four are conference and research papers, three from the
development years, on aerobraking and aerodynamic plane change, on aerodynamic orbital transfer and on the
vehicle's place in space control, and one from 2011 on the orbital test vehicle and its derivatives.
**The remaining four date from 2015 or later and are outside work**, an essay on
the vehicle and the weaponisation of space, a concept for a space station ambulance built on the vehicle's
technology, and two analyses of the vehicle's infrared observability and entry flow field written by people
with no access to the programme.

**The space agency's own reports on the vehicle stop in 2006**, two years after the transfer to the defence
research agency, and **no title in the survey describes a flown mission.** The vehicle has operated for
fifteen years, and the only later engineering paper on the vehicle itself is titled for the vehicle and its
derivatives rather than for any flight. The cluster also holds thirteen titles that do not name the X-37,
five on the Space Maneuver Vehicle and the X-40A from 1997 to 2002 and eight studies since 2007 that take the Space Maneuver Vehicle as the object of
trajectory optimisation, guidance or mission planning.

| Article | Vehicle | Why its cluster is thin |
|---|---|---|
| the X-33 article | X-33 | **Cancelled.** Sixty records, every one predating 2002 |
| the X-34 article | X-34 | **Cancelled.** The same shape, and two instances made it a pattern |
| the X-35 article | X-35 | **It won**, and contractor demonstrators flown for a source selection do not produce reports |
| the X-36 article | X-36 | **It produced a technique rather than a vehicle**, so its contribution is filed under the names of its methods |
| the X-37 article | X-37 | **It became classified.** It did not stop existing and it did not stop working. It stopped being publishable |

**The five reasons are entirely distinct and the conclusion is not that thin clusters mean failure.** The
X-37 is the most operationally successful vehicle in the last ten articles of this series and has the
thinnest trace of any of them.
**The documentary record measures the institution and its circumstances rather than the aircraft.**

### The Period Half and the Contemporary Half, Counted and Not Only Divided

**The research survey holds 4,827 research records drawn from Crossref, the NASA Technical Reports Server and the Defense Technical Information Center**,
of which 1,037 are report primaries, being 21.5 percent, by the identifier rule set out under The
Definition of Primary. **The median publication year is 2007.**

**Reporting a fraction alone is misleading, because adding a contemporary survey lowers the period fraction while leaving the period count untouched.**
Both are given.

| Half | Count | Share of dated |
|---|---|---|
| Period, through 2011 | 2,674 | 56.4 percent |
| Contemporary, 2012 onward | 2,067 | 43.6 percent |
| Undated | 86 | |
| **Total research records** | **4,827** | |

**The period count is 2,674 and the contemporary count is 2,067.** Both are given because a contemporary
survey lowers the period **share** while leaving the period **count** untouched, and reporting the share
alone reads as a regression when it is only the contemporary survey being added.

**A date is not a measure of primacy and this article reports both.** The technical report servers hold
original research reports almost exclusively, while a journal index holds originals, reviews and comment
together, so the report share is the closest available proxy for how much of the base is primary.

| Measure | Count | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Technical reports, all eras | 1,037 | 21.5 percent |
| Technical reports at or before 2011 | 867 | 18.0 percent |
| Journal and conference records | 3,790 | 78.5 percent |

A further **140** reference works are listed below, and they carry the relations that no journal article
states because every textbook does.
The count is the number of entries in that list.

### What the Record Does Not Contain

**No mass breakdown. No power budget. No propellant load. No thermal design. No description of any payload beyond the roughly ten experiments announced by name. No flight data of any kind from any of the eight missions.**
The article computes bounds precisely because none of these exists.

### The Reference Works

- [Hypersonic and High Temperature Gas Dynamics][book_hypersonic_and]

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a
report primary when its address is on the NASA Technical Reports Server or at the Defense Technical
Information Center, or it carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref
registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. By that rule 1,037 of the 4,827 research records
are report primaries, being 21.5 percent. **The space agency's reports on the vehicle are report primaries under that rule**,
and so are the agency's reports on the Shuttle orbiter and on aeroassisted transfer. **The rule does not
reach first-hand journal and conference papers**, such as the satellite drag analyses of the late 1950s and
the conference papers on the Space Maneuver Vehicle, so 21.5 percent is a lower bound on how much of the survey
is first-hand.

Primary sources for this article are the space agency reports published while the vehicle was being
designed, the Defense Technical Information Center holdings from the same window, and the journal and
conference papers contemporary with each relation the article uses.
**The programme's own operational record is not available at any level of primacy**, so the primary base is
a base for the physics rather than for the vehicle.

**A date and a primacy are different measurements and this article reports both**, because a cutoff
separates period from contemporary and says nothing whatever about whether a record is an original report or
a commentary on one. The technical report servers hold originals almost exclusively, so their share is the
closest available proxy, and it is given in the table above beside the date split rather than instead of it.

### Thin Subjects

**The subjects a technical argument rests on are not the subjects its vocabulary names**, and the gap
between the two is where a literature search fails. This article displays relations drawn from the second
zonal harmonic, the solar aspect angle, the square-cube law and the energy state approximation. Outside this
section the article's prose names the first and third where it uses them and never names the other two.
**A search built from what an article says will not find the literature the article depends on.**

Measured against the list of subjects the arguments actually use,
**eighteen of thirty-seven are thin or absent in the source base assembled here.** A subject counts as thin
when fewer than twelve dated records match its search terms or either half holds fewer than five. Thirteen are
named below, because a bare count invites the reader to assume the worst explanation. The other
five, orbital decay, plane change, bank angle modulation, radiative equilibrium wall temperature and
reusable tile protection, meet the same count and are not classified here.

**A subject can be thin for three reasons and a count cannot tell them apart.** Naming which applies is the
whole of the work.

**The heading is wrong, which is the commonest kind and the only curable one.** The field does not say
crossrange, it says lateral range and footprint. It does not say equilibrium glide, it says gliding entry
and cites Eggers and Allen. It did not say beta angle in 1968, it said solar aspect angle and sun incidence.
Counted in each field's own words rather than in this article's, equilibrium glide stands at eighteen records,
crossrange at fourteen, which takes it off the thin list, and vehicle scaling at eight.
**The records are present in the literature under the field's words**, and a question put in the article's
words does not reach them.

**That is worth stating plainly, because it applies to the instrument as much as to the search.** A count of
how well a subject is covered is itself a search, and it undercounts for exactly the same reason.
**A thin result is a claim about the question before it is a claim about the field.**

**The knowledge is settled and stopped generating papers**, which is not curable and must not be padded. The
vis-viva relation stands at zero records, the rocket equation at one and Kepler's third law at three.
**These are not gaps.** They are relations that appear in every
astrodynamics textbook and in no journal article, because nobody has published on them since the seventeenth
and nineteenth centuries respectively.
**The reference works section carries them and that is the correct home.**

**The work was never done**, which is rare and has to be argued and never assumed. Nothing in this article's
subject list falls into it.

**What remains thin, and which kind each is.**

| Subject | Period | Contemporary | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Specific orbital energy | 0 | 0 | **Settled.** Every astrodynamics textbook, no journal article |
| The rocket equation | 0 | 1 | **Settled.** Same, and the [X-34][related_post_a331_orbital_sciences_x34] article found the same |
| Kepler and the orbital period | 1 | 2 | **Settled**, and the relation is from 1619 |
| Energy height | 1 | 0 | **Settled.** The method is named after a 1954 paper and is textbook thereafter |
| The beta angle, period half | 0 | 1 | **Thin heading, and the period's own words do not find it either.** The period documented the same geometry inside thermal design reports that name neither the angle nor its modern synonyms |
| Aerobraking corridor control | 4 | 2 | **Thin heading.** The subject is covered by 565 dated records whose title or venue names aerobraking, aerocapture or aeroassist |
| Stagnation heating, contemporary half | 50 | 0 | **Thin heading.** Modern work computes the same quantity and does not cite the correlations by name |
| Manoeuvre detection, period half | 0 | 19 | **Genuinely modern.** The capability to detect a manoeuvre from the ground is recent |
| Debris disposal, period half | 4 | 64 | **Genuinely modern.** Disposal became an obligation in this century, having been a courtesy before it |
| Albedo and Earth infrared, contemporary half | 12 | 2 | **Not classified.** Albedo also names the albedo of Mars and the gamma-ray albedo of the Earth, whose records are excluded, and the two that remain do not show which reason applies |

**The vehicle's own subject is thin by this count, and only just**, with seventeen period and four contemporary records
whose title or venue names the X-37 or its programme, and that is why the section above sets the records out
one by one. **The contemporary half falls one short of the threshold, and the four contemporary records are outside work that names the vehicle, none of them reporting a flight.**
Every other subject here has an ordinary explanation. The vehicle's own is the only one whose cause is that
somebody decided the work should not be published.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject.**
Its 4,827 records come from NASA's Technical Reports Server, the Defense Technical Information Center and the
Crossref index of the journal literature. Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a
record that shares only such a word, or whose only link to the vehicle is a distant application of a shared
technique, is excluded. An orbiter also names the planetary and lunar missions and their navigation, gravity
science and instruments, an orbital also names a molecular or electronic orbital, and an orbit also names the
eye socket. A radiator or a heat pipe also names the cooling of buildings, vehicles, processors and data
centres, a battery life cycle also names the recycling and environmental assessment of a battery, and a solar
cell also names the device physics of terrestrial photovoltaics and the arrays of airships and uncrewed
aircraft. Stagnation flow also names the low-speed flows of jets, plates and stretching sheets, radiative
equilibrium also names radiation in gases and enclosures, and an eclipse also names astronomy, public outreach
and a software platform. The ionosphere and the magnetosphere share the altitudes but not the neutral density
that sets drag, a re-entry vehicle also names the warhead of a ballistic missile whose radar tracking is a
defence subject, and autonomous landing also names multirotor aircraft settling on moving platforms.
Communication and navigation constellations, terrestrial wireless power transfer, dual-use technology outside
space, and secrecy in fiction, foreign policy and public relations are excluded on the same ground.
Correction, erratum and retraction notices, withdrawal notices, figure and supplementary-material records,
peer-review reports and journal front matter such as subject indexes are excluded as well, because a survey
counts research works and those are parts of works or editorial events rather than works. A document
deposited twice is counted once. Book reviews, prefaces and forewords to collections, patent abstracts, the
abstracts that abstract journals and the abstract sections of other journals reprint, and news items, signed
or unsigned, are excluded on the same ground, and so is a news writer's reply to a letter about a news story,
which belongs to the news item. A signed comment on a paper, a discussion of a paper, the author's reply to
either and a signed letter on a research subject are research works, because each argues about a result, and
they are admitted when their subject is this article's.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** The cycle life and state of health of electric vehicle and
grid storage batteries, laboratory studies of loop and pulsating heat pipes that name no application,
control of air-breathing hypersonic vehicles, and the subsystems of the Shuttle orbiter that an uncrewed
vehicle shares each share a relation, a technique or a hardware lineage with this subject, so each is kept
and a reader may weigh it accordingly.

**No residual cluster is needed.** Every admitted record belongs to one of the 24 named clusters, each
named for what its titles are, so no cluster holds records admitted only because they fit nowhere else.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.**
A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

## Epistemic State

### Historical Fact

The programme began at the space agency in 1999 with Boeing as contractor, transferred to the Defense
Advanced Research Projects Agency on 13 September 2004, and the Air Force announced its own derivative on 17
November 2006. The X-40A was an 80 percent scale drop-test vehicle and the X-37 is a 120 percent scaled
derivative of it. The Approach and Landing Test Vehicle first flew on 7 April 2006 and its first free flight
ended in a runway excursion. Eight orbital missions have launched since 22 April 2010, of which seven have
landed, totalling 4,208.65 days. The sixth mission lasted 908.88 days. The seventh flew a highly elliptical
orbit catalogued at 336 by 37,895 kilometres and an inclination of 59.27 degrees, and the Space Force announced
in October 2024 that it would use aerobraking to change that orbit and dispose of its service module. The
published dimensions are 8.92 metres long, 4.55 metres in span, 2.90 metres high, with a payload bay of 2.1
by 1.2 metres and a launch mass of 4,990 kilograms. Those dimensions, the launch mass and the mission times
rest on the [encyclopaedic specification][ref_x37], which compiles Air Force, Boeing and press figures, and
the orbits rest on a single catalogue \[[General Catalog of Artificial Space Objects][ref_gcat]\].

### Engineering Analysis

Every quantitative result in this article is computed from those published figures and from standard
relations. The orbital period, circular speed, eclipse fraction, full-sun beta threshold,
nodal precession, beta cycle and orbit count follow from the published altitude and inclination alone. The
scaling exponents and the duty cycle follow from published dimensions, masses and dates, and involve no
model whatever. The array and radiator bounds follow from the published bay dimensions. The drag figures
follow from a piecewise exponential atmosphere at nominal solar activity. The aerobraking figures follow
from the published orbit.
**The identity showing that entry heading change is independent of mass, area and atmosphere is exact within the equilibrium glide assumption**,
and agrees with an integration that retains the term it claims cancels.

### Inference

The node and beta cycles are short against the mission, at 63.31 and 53.95 days against 908.88, and from
that the article infers that the eclipse average describes what the mission experienced rather than a
modelling convenience. That the square-cube penalty rather than a design choice explains the payload fraction is an
inference from the measured mass exponent of 1.924, and other explanations are available.

The inference that endurance rather than propulsion is the binding constraint comes from the computed drag
budget being small at the altitudes flown. That heat rejection binds more tightly than power generation is
an inference from two bounds whose ranges overlap at the low end. A walk-down calculation using an assumed
ballistic coefficient is the basis for inferring that the aerobraking campaign required a perigee near 100
kilometres. That the programme's documentary silence is caused by classification rather than by inactivity
is an inference from the pattern of the space agency's twelve reports on the vehicle, which stop in 2006, two
years after the transfer to the defence research agency.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**What the vehicle carries, what it does, and why the missions run as long as they do.** Also the actual
electrical load, propellant load and drag area, the perigee flown during the aerobraking
campaign, the fraction of the seventh mission's apogee reduction that was aerodynamic, and whether the
published specification is complete.
**The article is a set of bounds and identities consistent with the public record, and a classified programme is entitled to have a public record that does not fully describe it.**

## Out of Scope

The detailed design of the Approach and Landing Test Vehicle's flight control system. The Atlas V, Falcon 9
and Falcon Heavy launch vehicles and their performance to the orbits flown. The legal and treaty questions
raised by a manoeuvrable military vehicle in orbit, which are a substantial literature in their own right
and are surveyed here without being analysed. The Chinese and other reusable spaceplane programmes that have
flown since 2020, which deserve separate treatment. The economics of reusable launch, treated in the
[X-33][related_post_a330_lockheed_martin_x33] and [X-34][related_post_a331_orbital_sciences_x34] articles.
The detailed chemistry of TUFROC and its successors.

## Conclusion

**The X-37B answered a question about endurance. Endurance in orbit turns out to be cheap once the power loop is sized for it.**
A 908-day mission is 14,140 charge and discharge cycles, which on the cycle-life law assumed here a battery
cycled to something between 38 and 50 percent depth of discharge will survive, at a mass penalty of roughly
fifteen kilograms for each kilowatt
of continuous load. The drag makeup over the same mission is between 23 and 152 kilograms of propellant at
the altitudes flown. **That neither number is large for a five-tonne vehicle is the finding.** The
obstacle to a very long orbital mission was never physics. It was the willingness to build a vehicle that
had nothing else to do.

**The vehicle's second answer concerns manoeuvre, and it came from the atmosphere rather than the engine.**
Lowering perigee for twenty-four metres per second bought nearly two and a half kilometres per second of
apogee reduction, a leverage of 103 to one, and did it at a fifth of the heat flux of a full entry.
**A vehicle whose entire propulsive budget is 311 metres per second performed a 2,449 metre per second manoeuvre**,
and the only reason it could is that it has a thermal protection system and therefore may touch the
atmosphere without consequence. **Reusability bought manoeuvrability**, an argument not usually
made for it.

**Two smaller results deserve carrying forward because neither needed a model.** Measuring the exponent that
relates this vehicle to the Shuttle orbiter puts mass at length to the **1.924** against 3 for geometric
similarity, so
**a similar orbiter shrunk to 8.92 metres would mass 1,072 kilograms and this one masses 4,990**. The small
vehicle keeps the airframe and loses the room, so the payload fraction is 4.55 percent and needs
no apology. And the operational claim is not the longest mission but the **77.46 percent duty cycle** across
the 5,433 days from first launch to seventh landing.
**Two airframes held an X-37B in orbit for three quarters of fifteen years**, and the record
mission conceals that turnaround.

**The third answer is about the record itself, and it is uncomfortable.** No vehicle in the
last ten articles of this series has been more successful, and none has left a thinner documentary trace.
Twenty titles in a survey of 4,827 records, none describing a flown mission, and the
space agency's reports on the vehicle stop in 2006 while the vehicle went on to fly orbital missions for
fifteen years from 2010.
**Four previous articles found a thin cluster for four different reasons, all of which were forms of the programme ending. This one is thin because the programme succeeded and was classified.**

**The documentary trace measures the institution rather than the aircraft**, and an outside analyst armed
with published dimensions, public orbital elements and a textbook can recover the vehicle's scale, its power
budget, its endurance mechanism and the arithmetic of its most novel manoeuvre.
**What that analyst cannot recover is the only thing the programme was built to do**, and the gap fairly
summarises what classification achieves and what it costs.

## Equations

<!-- Equations generated by _lib/equations.py from _sources/equations/. Edit the data file and regenerate. Do not edit this section by hand. -->

This section collects the 64 display equations of the article in the order they appear,
each under its number and reproduced exactly as it stands in the text.
A title in bold names an established result,
and a title in italics beginning with the word Bespoke names a construction made for this analysis.
Of the 64, 46 are established and 18 are bespoke.
All relations are evaluated in the International System, with altitudes and orbital radii quoted in kilometres and heat fluxes in watts per square centimetre in the tables, and the article's own notation table resolves the colliding symbols, so $\mathcal{E}$ is the specific orbital energy while $\varepsilon$ is the emissivity, $a$ is the semi-major axis, $\delta$ is the depth of discharge while $\delta_{\odot}$ is the solar declination, $T$ is the orbital period while every temperature carries a subscript, and $N_{\text{orb}}$ and $N_{\text{cyc}}$ are counted separately though shown to coincide.

**Equation 1, Specific Energy of a Keplerian Orbit.**
The specific orbital energy is the kinetic less the potential energy per unit mass and depends only on the semi-major axis.

$$
\mathcal{E} = \frac{v^{2}}{2} - \frac{\mu}{r} = -\frac{\mu}{2a}
\tag{1}
$$

**Equation 2, Reciprocals of the Published Scale Factors.**
The reciprocal of the 80 percent figure is 1.25 and that of the 120 percent figure is 0.833, so the two published ratios are not reciprocals of each other.
[Boeing X-37][ref_x37]

$$
\frac{1}{0.80} = 1.25, \qquad \frac{1}{1.20} = 0.833,
\tag{2}
$$

**Equation 3, Period of a Circular Orbit.**
The period of a circular orbit is two pi times the square root of the cube of the radius over the gravitational parameter.
[orbital period][ref_orbital_period]

$$
T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{r^{3}}{\mu}}
\tag{3}
$$

**Equation 4, Circular Orbital Speed.**
The circular speed is the square root of the gravitational parameter over the radius.
[orbital period][ref_orbital_period]

$$
v_{c} = \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{r}}
\tag{4}
$$

**Equation 5, Eclipse Fraction of a Circular Orbit in a Cylindrical Shadow.**
Treating the shadow as a cylinder, which neglects the penumbra, the fraction of the orbit in eclipse follows from the radius, the Earth radius and the beta angle.
[beta angle][ref_beta_angle]

$$
f_{E} = \frac{1}{\pi} \arccos\!\left( \frac{\sqrt{r^{2} - R_{\oplus}^{2}}}{r \cos \beta} \right)
\tag{5}
$$

**Equation 6, Beta Angle Above Which Eclipse Vanishes.**
The eclipse vanishes when the beta angle exceeds the inverse sine of the Earth radius over the orbital radius.
[beta angle][ref_beta_angle]

$$
\beta > \beta^{*} = \arcsin\!\left( \frac{R_{\oplus}}{r} \right)
\tag{6}
$$

**Equation 7, Largest Reachable Beta Angle.**
The largest beta angle at an inclination is the inclination plus the obliquity of the ecliptic, which for the catalogued inclinations stays below the full-sun threshold.
[General Catalog of Artificial Space Objects][ref_gcat]

$$
\beta_{\max} = i + 23.44^{\circ}, \qquad 43.49^{\circ} + 23.44^{\circ} = 66.93^{\circ}, \qquad 45.08^{\circ} + 23.44^{\circ} = 68.52^{\circ} \;<\; \beta^{*} = 70.22^{\circ},
\tag{7}
$$

*Equation 8, Bespoke Mean Eclipse Fraction Over Node and Season.*
The eclipse fraction is averaged over a uniform grid of 720 node positions and 60 solar longitudes, a sampling the article constructs.

$$
\bar{f}_{E} = \frac{1}{J K} \sum_{j=1}^{J} \sum_{k=1}^{K} f_{E}\!\left( \beta(\Omega_{j}, \lambda_{k}) \right), \qquad J = 720, \quad K = 60,
\tag{8}
$$

**Equation 9, Nodal Regression Due to the Second Zonal Harmonic.**
The dominant secular effect of the Earth's oblateness regresses the ascending node of a near-circular orbit at a rate set by the second zonal harmonic, the radius and the inclination.

$$
\dot{\Omega} = -\frac{3}{2} J_{2} \left( \frac{R_{\oplus}}{p} \right)^{2} \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{a^{3}}} \, \cos i
\tag{9}
$$

**Equation 10, Beta Angle From the Sun Vector and Orbit Normal.**
The sine of the beta angle follows from the solar declination and right ascension, the inclination and the node.

$$
\sin \beta = \cos \delta_{\odot} \sin i \sin(\Omega - \alpha_{\odot}) + \sin \delta_{\odot} \cos i
\tag{10}
$$

**Equation 11, Beat Period of the Beta Angle.**
The beta angle geometry repeats at the beat between the nodal regression and the Sun's annual motion.

$$
T_{\beta} = \frac{360^{\circ}}{\lvert \dot{\Omega} - \dot{\lambda}_{\odot} \rvert}
\tag{11}
$$

*Equation 12, Bespoke Orbit Count of the Sixth Mission.*
The published mission duration over the period of a circular orbit at 400 kilometres, the representative altitude the article takes for the catalogued orbit, gives 14,140 orbits.

$$
N_{\text{orb}} = \frac{t_{\text{mission}}}{T} = \frac{908.88 \times 86{,}400}{5{,}553.6} = 14{,}140
\tag{12}
$$

**Equation 13, Planform Area of the Payload Bay.**
The published bay dimensions of 2.1 by 1.2 metres give 2.52 square metres.
[Boeing X-37][ref_x37]

$$
A_{\text{bay}} = 2.1 \times 1.2 = 2.52 \ \text{square metres}.
\tag{13}
$$

**Equation 14, Power of a Sun-Pointed Array.**
A sun-pointed array generates the solar constant times its area times the cell efficiency times the packing factor.

$$
P_{\text{array}} = S \, A \, \eta \, \kappa
\tag{14}
$$

**Equation 15, Array to Load Power Ratio With Eclipse Recharge.**
An array carrying a continuous load must also recharge the battery in sunlight, so its power exceeds the load by a term in the eclipse fraction and the charge and discharge efficiencies.

$$
\frac{P_{\text{array}}}{P_{\text{load}}} = 1 + \frac{f_{E}}{(1 - f_{E})\,\eta_{c}\,\eta_{d}}
\tag{15}
$$

*Equation 16, Bespoke Continuous Load Supported by a Six Square Metre Array.*
The load is evaluated for an assumed array of six square metres, cell efficiency of 0.30, packing factor of 0.85 and charge and discharge efficiencies of 0.90.

$$
P_{\text{load}} = \frac{S \, A \, \eta \, \kappa}{P_{\text{array}} / P_{\text{load}}} = \frac{1{,}361 \times 6 \times 0.30 \times 0.85}{1.7896} = \frac{2{,}082.3}{1.7896} = 1{,}164 \ \text{watts},
\tag{16}
$$

**Equation 17, Net Radiative Flux From a Radiator.**
A radiator rejects its emissivity times the Stefan-Boltzmann constant times the difference of the fourth powers of its temperature and the sink temperature.
[Stefan-Boltzmann constant][ref_stefan_boltzmann]

$$
q = \varepsilon \sigma \left( T_{r}^{4} - T_{s}^{4} \right)
\tag{17}
$$

**Equation 18, Effective Sink Temperature Near the Earth.**
The sink temperature follows from the balance of emitted radiation against absorbed outgoing longwave flux and reflected sunlight over the view factor to the Earth.
[Stefan-Boltzmann constant][ref_stefan_boltzmann]

$$
T_{s} = \left( \frac{F \left( \varepsilon q_{\text{IR}} + \alpha_{\oplus} \alpha_{s} S \right)}{\varepsilon \sigma} \right)^{1/4}
\tag{18}
$$

**Equation 19, Radiator Area for a Given Dissipation.**
Inverting the net flux gives the radiator area a given dissipation demands.

$$
A_{r} = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon \sigma \left( T_{r}^{4} - T_{s}^{4} \right)}
\tag{19}
$$

*Equation 20, Bespoke Heat Rejected by the Payload Bay Doors.*
The door rejection uses an assumed emissivity of 0.85, a sink temperature from an assumed view factor of one half, and assumed radiator temperatures of 20 and 40 degrees Celsius.

$$
Q_{\text{flat}} = 2 \times (2.1 \times 0.6) \times 214.40 = 540 \ \text{watts}, \qquad Q_{\text{curved}} = 2 \times 2.52 \times 321.935 = 1{,}623 \ \text{watts},
\tag{20}
$$

**Equation 21, Battery Energy Drawn in One Eclipse.**
The energy drawn from the battery is the load times the eclipse duration over the discharge efficiency.

$$
E = \frac{P_{\text{load}} \, t_{E}}{\eta_{d}}
\tag{21}
$$

**Equation 22, Installed Capacity and Battery Mass.**
The installed capacity is the energy drawn over the depth of discharge, and the mass is that capacity over the cell specific energy.

$$
C = \frac{E}{\delta}, \qquad m_{b} = \frac{E}{\delta \, w} = \frac{P_{\text{load}} \, t_{E}}{\eta_{d} \, \delta \, w}.
\tag{22}
$$

**Equation 23, Inverse Power Law of Cycle Life.**
The standard empirical form for a secondary cell in low Earth orbit makes cycle life inversely proportional to a power of the depth of discharge.
[Rickman][research_stevenlrickman]

$$
N_{\text{cyc}} \, \delta^{k} = \text{constant}, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \frac{N_{\text{cyc}}}{N_{\text{ref}}} = \left( \frac{\delta_{\text{ref}}}{\delta} \right)^{k}
\tag{23}
$$

**Equation 24, Admissible Depth of Discharge for a Cycle Count.**
Inverting the power law gives the depth of discharge that a required cycle count admits relative to a reference point.

$$
\delta = \delta_{\text{ref}} \left( \frac{N_{\text{ref}}}{N_{\text{cyc}}} \right)^{1/k}
\tag{24}
$$

*Equation 25, Bespoke Admissible Depth of Discharge for the Sixth Mission.*
The power law is anchored at an assumed reference of 30,000 cycles at 30 percent and evaluated at the extreme exponents of 1.5 and 3.

$$
\delta_{k=3} = 0.30 \left( \frac{30{,}000}{14{,}140} \right)^{1/3} = 0.385, \qquad \delta_{k=1.5} = 0.30 \left( \frac{30{,}000}{14{,}140} \right)^{1/1.5} = 0.495,
\tag{25}
$$

**Equation 26, Drag Deceleration.**
The drag deceleration is the dynamic pressure times the drag coefficient and reference area over the mass.
[ballistic coefficient][ref_ballistic_coefficient]

$$
a_{D} = \frac{1}{2} \rho v^{2} \frac{C_{D} A_{\text{ref}}}{m}
\tag{26}
$$

**Equation 27, Drag Makeup Over a Mission.**
Holding the orbit at constant density costs the dynamic pressure over the ballistic coefficient, multiplied by the mission duration.
[ballistic coefficient][ref_ballistic_coefficient]

$$
\Delta v = \frac{\rho v^{2}}{2 B} \, t.
\tag{27}
$$

*Equation 28, Bespoke Ballistic Coefficient of the X-37B.*
The published launch mass is divided by a drag area of eight square metres that the article assumes.
[Boeing X-37][ref_x37]

$$
B = \frac{m}{C_{D} A_{\text{ref}}} = \frac{4{,}990}{8} = 623.75 \ \text{kilograms per square metre},
\tag{28}
$$

*Equation 29, Bespoke Drag Makeup at 400 Kilometres.*
The makeup over the sixth mission is evaluated with the assumed ballistic coefficient and a nominal piecewise exponential density model.

$$
\Delta v = \frac{3.725 \times 10^{-12} \times 7{,}668.6^{2}}{2 \times 623.75} \times 7.853 \times 10^{7} = 13.79 \ \text{metres per second}.
\tag{29}
$$

**Equation 30, Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation and Propellant Fraction.**
The velocity increment is the effective exhaust velocity times the logarithm of the mass ratio, and inverting it gives the propellant fraction.
[rocket equation][ref_rocket_equation]

$$
\Delta v = I_{sp} \, g_{0} \ln \frac{m_{0}}{m_{0} - m_{p}}, \qquad \frac{m_{p}}{m_{0}} = 1 - \exp\!\left( -\frac{\Delta v}{I_{sp} g_{0}} \right)
\tag{30}
$$

*Equation 31, Bespoke Propulsive Budget of the X-37B.*
The rocket equation is evaluated for a propellant load of 500 kilograms at a specific impulse of 300 seconds, both values the article assumes.
[rocket equation][ref_rocket_equation]

$$
\Delta v_{\text{budget}} = 300 \times 9.80665 \times \ln \frac{4{,}990}{4{,}990 - 500} = 2{,}942.0 \times 0.10558 = 310.6 \ \text{metres per second}.
\tag{31}
$$

*Equation 32, Bespoke Propellant for Drag Makeup at 300 and 400 Kilometres.*
The propellant fraction is evaluated at the assumed specific impulse for the makeup increments that rest on the assumed ballistic coefficient.

$$
m_{p}^{300} = 4{,}990 \left[ 1 - e^{-90.85 / (300 \times 9.80665)} \right] = 151.7, \qquad m_{p}^{400} = 4{,}990 \left[ 1 - e^{-13.79 / (300 \times 9.80665)} \right] = 23.3
\tag{32}
$$

*Equation 33, Bespoke Penalty of Letting the Orbit Decay.*
The ratio of the makeup for a decaying orbit to that for a held orbit rests on the assumed ballistic coefficient and the nominal density model.

$$
\frac{\Delta v_{\text{decay}}}{\Delta v_{\text{hold}}} = \frac{18.47}{13.79} = 1.339,
\tag{33}
$$

**Equation 34, Secular Decay of the Semi-Major Axis Under Drag.**
Equating the rate of change of orbital energy to the work done by drag gives the rate at which the semi-major axis decays.

$$
\frac{d\mathcal{E}}{dt} = -a_{D} v = \frac{\mu}{2a^{2}} \frac{da}{dt} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \frac{da}{dt} = -\frac{2 a^{2} v}{\mu} \, a_{D}
\tag{34}
$$

**Equation 35, Linearity of the Makeup in Density.**
Because the makeup requirement is linear in density, scaling the density by a multiplier scales the requirement by the same multiplier.

$$
\Delta v = \frac{\rho v^{2}}{2 B} t \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \frac{\Delta v(\zeta \rho)}{\Delta v(\rho)} = \zeta
\tag{35}
$$

**Equation 36, Sutton and Graves Stagnation-Point Heat Flux.**
The convective stagnation-point flux is a constant times the square root of density over nose radius times the cube of speed.
[Sutton and Graves][ref_sutton_graves]

$$
\dot{q}_{s} = k \sqrt{\frac{\rho}{R_{n}}} \, v^{3}
\tag{36}
$$

**Equation 37, Radiative Equilibrium Wall Temperature.**
A surface in radiative equilibrium reaches the fourth root of the heat flux over the emissivity times the Stefan-Boltzmann constant.

$$
T_{w} = \left( \frac{\dot{q}_{s}}{\varepsilon \sigma} \right)^{1/4}.
\tag{37}
$$

**Equation 38, Vertical Force Balance in Equilibrium Glide.**
In equilibrium glide the vertical component of lift balances weight less centrifugal relief.
[equilibrium glide][ref_equilibrium_glide]

$$
L \cos \phi = m \left( g - \frac{v^{2}}{r} \right)
\tag{38}
$$

**Equation 39, Heading Rate in Equilibrium Glide.**
The horizontal component of lift turns the velocity vector at a rate set by the bank angle and the gravity less centrifugal term.
[equilibrium glide][ref_equilibrium_glide]

$$
\frac{d\psi}{dt} = \frac{\left( g - v^{2}/r \right) \tan \phi}{v}
\tag{39}
$$

**Equation 40, Deceleration in Equilibrium Glide.**
The deceleration is the lift divided by the lift-to-drag ratio, expressed through the vertical balance.

$$
\frac{dv}{dt} = -\frac{1}{L/D} \cdot \frac{g - v^{2}/r}{\cos \phi}.
\tag{40}
$$

**Equation 41, Heading Change Independent of Altitude.**
At constant lift-to-drag ratio and bank angle, dividing the heading rate by the deceleration removes the altitude term, so the heading change depends only on those two and the speed ratio.

$$
\frac{d\psi}{dv} = -\frac{(L/D) \sin \phi}{v}, \qquad \Delta\psi = (L/D) \sin \phi \, \ln\!\left( \frac{v_{i}}{v_{f}} \right).
\tag{41}
$$

**Equation 42, Time Element in the Velocity Domain.**
The equilibrium-glide deceleration supplies the element of time as a function of speed.

$$
dt = -\frac{dv}{a_{D}}, \qquad a_{D} = \frac{1}{L/D} \cdot \frac{g - v^{2}/r}{\cos \phi}
\tag{42}
$$

**Equation 43, Crossrange and Downrange Integrals.**
The crossrange and downrange are the two components of the ground track integrated over speed.

$$
y = \int_{v_{f}}^{v_{i}} \frac{v \sin \psi(v)}{a_{D}(v)} \, dv, \qquad x = \int_{v_{f}}^{v_{i}} \frac{v \cos \psi(v)}{a_{D}(v)} \, dv
\tag{43}
$$

*Equation 44, Bespoke Constant-Bank Crossrange Against the Shuttle Requirement.*
Taking a hypersonic lift-to-drag ratio of 1.1 as representative of the orbiter, the constant-bank crossrange is 0.686 of the 1,100 nautical mile requirement.
[The Space Shuttle Decision][ref_shuttle_decision]

$$
y = \frac{1{,}397.8 \ \text{km}}{1.852 \ \text{km per nautical mile}} = 754.7 \ \text{nautical miles}, \qquad \frac{754.7}{1{,}100} = 0.686 .
\tag{44}
$$

*Equation 45, Bespoke Sensitivity of Crossrange to the Terminal Speed.*
Moving the terminal speed, a modelling choice the article makes, from 700 to 1,200 metres per second changes the crossrange by 2.9 percent.

$$
\frac{y(700) - y(1{,}200)}{y(900)} = \frac{1{,}411 - 1{,}371}{1{,}397.8} = 0.029 .
\tag{45}
$$

**Equation 46, Plane Change Between Circular Orbits.**
Two circular orbits of equal radius are joined by an isosceles velocity triangle, so the plane change costs twice the speed times the sine of half the inclination change.

$$
\Delta v = 2 v \sin\!\left( \frac{\Delta i}{2} \right).
\tag{46}
$$

**Equation 47, Glide Range.**
A glide trades height for distance at the lift-to-drag ratio.

$$
R = \left( \frac{L}{D} \right) h
\tag{47}
$$

**Equation 48, Energy Height.**
The energy height is the altitude plus the kinetic energy expressed as a height.

$$
h_{E} = h + \frac{v^{2}}{2 g}.
\tag{48}
$$

**Equation 49, Scaling Exponent Between Two Vehicles.**
For a quantity that scales as a power of a length, the exponent is the ratio of the logarithms of the two quantity and length ratios.

$$
Q \propto \ell^{\,n} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad n = \frac{\ln \left( Q_{1} / Q_{2} \right)}{\ln \left( \ell_{1} / \ell_{2} \right)}
\tag{49}
$$

**Equation 50, Mass of a Geometrically Similar Orbiter.**
Scaling the Shuttle orbiter's launch mass by the cube of the length ratio, the cube law of geometric similarity at constant density, gives 1,072 kilograms against the X-37B's 4,990.

$$
m_{\text{similar}} = 78{,}000 \left( \frac{8.92}{37.24} \right)^{3} = 1{,}072 \ \text{kilograms}, \qquad \frac{4{,}990}{1{,}072} = 4.655 .
\tag{50}
$$

**Equation 51, Payload Fraction.**
The published payload capacity over the launch mass gives a payload fraction of 4.55 percent.
[Boeing X-37][ref_x37]

$$
\frac{m_{\text{payload}}}{m_{\text{launch}}} = \frac{227}{4{,}990} = 4.55 \ \text{percent}.
\tag{51}
$$

**Equation 52, Fleet Duty Cycle.**
The summed durations of the seven completed missions over the span from first launch to seventh landing give a duty cycle of 77.46 percent.
[Boeing X-37][ref_x37]

$$
\Phi = \frac{\sum_{k} t_{k}}{t_{\text{span}}} = \frac{4{,}208.65}{5{,}433} = 77.46 \text{ percent}
\tag{52}
$$

**Equation 53, Semi-Major Axis, Eccentricity and Semi-Latus Rectum From the Apsides.**
The catalogued perigee and apogee radii fix the semi-major axis, the eccentricity and the semi-latus rectum.
[General Catalog of Artificial Space Objects][ref_gcat]

$$
a = \frac{r_{p} + r_{a}}{2}, \qquad e = \frac{r_{a} - r_{p}}{r_{a} + r_{p}}, \qquad p = a \left( 1 - e^{2} \right)
\tag{53}
$$

**Equation 54, Vis-Viva Relation.**
The speed at any point on an orbit follows from the gravitational parameter, the radius and the semi-major axis.
[vis-viva][ref_vis_viva]

$$
v = \sqrt{\mu \left( \frac{2}{r} - \frac{1}{a} \right)}
\tag{54}
$$

**Equation 55, Velocity Removed by Aerobraking.**
The difference between the perigee speed of the catalogued elliptical orbit and the circular speed at that altitude is 2,448.8 metres per second.
[vis-viva][ref_vis_viva]

$$
\Delta v = v_{p} - v_{c} = 2{,}448.8 \text{ metres per second}.
\tag{55}
$$

*Equation 56, Bespoke Cost of Lowering Perigee to 100 Kilometres.*
Lowering perigee to 100 kilometres, a target altitude the article assumes, costs the difference of two apogee speeds from the vis-viva relation.

$$
\Delta v_{\text{lower}} = \sqrt{\mu \left( \frac{2}{r_{a}} - \frac{1}{25{,}493.6} \right)} - \sqrt{\mu \left( \frac{2}{r_{a}} - \frac{1}{25{,}375.6} \right)} = 1{,}539.85 - 1{,}516.06 = 23.79 \ \text{metres per second}.
\tag{56}
$$

*Equation 57, Bespoke Leverage of Aerobraking.*
The velocity the atmosphere removes over the cost of lowering perigee to the assumed 100 kilometres gives a leverage of 102.9.

$$
\frac{v_{p} - v_{c}}{\Delta v_{\text{lower}}} = \frac{2{,}448.8}{23.79} = 102.9 .
\tag{57}
$$

**Equation 58, Velocity Removed per Perigee Pass.**
The decrement per pass is the drag deceleration integrated along the arc, written with the true anomaly as the independent variable.

$$
\Delta v_{\text{pass}} = \int \frac{\rho(r) \, v^{2}}{2 B} \, dt = \int_{-\nu_{0}}^{\nu_{0}} \frac{\rho(r) \, v^{2}}{2 B} \cdot \frac{r^{2}}{\sqrt{\mu p}} \, d\nu
\tag{58}
$$

**Equation 59, Apogee After One Pass.**
Inverting the vis-viva relation at the reduced perigee speed gives the new semi-major axis and apogee radius.

$$
a' = \left( \frac{2}{r_{p}} - \frac{(v_{p} - \Delta v_{\text{pass}})^{2}}{\mu} \right)^{-1}, \qquad r_{a}' = 2 a' - r_{p}.
\tag{59}
$$

*Equation 60, Bespoke Fixed-Period Estimate of the Required Decrement.*
Holding the initial period constant over roughly 150 days gives about 320 passes and a demanded 7.65 metres per second per pass.

$$
N = \frac{150 \times 24}{11.253} = 319.9, \qquad \frac{2{,}448.8}{319.9} = 7.65 \ \text{metres per second},
\tag{60}
$$

*Equation 61, Bespoke Walk-Down Times Against the Calendar.*
The walk-down computed with the assumed ballistic coefficient and nominal density places the roughly 150 days available between the times at 100 and 110 kilometres.

$$
99.7 \ \text{days} \;<\; 150 \ \text{days} \;<\; 480.7 \ \text{days}.
\tag{61}
$$

*Equation 62, Bespoke Heating on an Aerobraking Pass.*
The stagnation flux and wall temperature are evaluated at the assumed 100 kilometre perigee, an assumed nose radius of 0.30 metres and an assumed emissivity of 0.85.

$$
\dot{q}_{s} = 1.7415 \times 10^{-4} \sqrt{\frac{5.297 \times 10^{-7}}{0.30}} \, (10{,}361.1)^{3} = 2.574 \times 10^{5} \ \text{W/m}^{2}, \qquad T_{w} = \left( \frac{\dot{q}_{s}}{0.85 \, \sigma} \right)^{1/4} = 1{,}520 \ \text{K},
\tag{62}
$$

**Equation 63, Pass Count Proportional to the Ballistic Coefficient.**
Because the drag integral carries the ballistic coefficient as a single divisor, the number of passes at a fixed perigee is proportional to it.

$$
\Delta v_{\text{pass}} \propto \frac{1}{B} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad N_{\text{passes}} \propto B
\tag{63}
$$

*Equation 64, Bespoke Ballistic Coefficient of the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.*
The published drag area and mass are combined with a drag coefficient of 2.0 that the article assumes for free molecular flow.
[Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Operational Aerobraking Phase Assessment][ref_mro_aerobraking]

$$
B_{\text{MRO}} = \frac{1{,}400}{2.0 \times 37.5} = 18.7 \ \text{kilograms per square metre}, \qquad \frac{B_{\text{X-37B}}}{B_{\text{MRO}}} = \frac{623.75}{18.67} = 33.4 .
\tag{64}
$$

### Notation

- $\mathcal{E}$, the specific orbital energy
- $\mu$, the gravitational parameter of the Earth
- $a$, the semi-major axis
- $v_{c}$, the circular orbital speed
- $R_{\oplus}$, the equatorial radius of the Earth
- $f_{E}$, the eclipse fraction, with $\bar{f}_{E}$ its mean over node and season
- $\beta$, the beta angle, with $\beta^{*}$ the threshold above which eclipse vanishes
- $J_{2}$, the second zonal harmonic of the Earth's gravity field
- $\dot{\Omega}$, the rate of nodal regression
- $T_{\beta}$, the beat period of the beta angle
- $N_{\text{orb}}$, the number of orbits, with $N_{\text{cyc}}$ the number of battery cycles
- $P_{\text{array}}$, the array power, with $P_{\text{load}}$ the continuous load
- $\eta$, the cell efficiency, with $\eta_{c}$ and $\eta_{d}$ the charge and discharge efficiencies
- $\kappa$, the packing factor of the array
- $\varepsilon$, the emissivity
- $\sigma$, the Stefan-Boltzmann constant
- $T_{s}$, the sink temperature, with $T_{r}$ the radiator temperature and $T_{w}$ the wall temperature
- $\alpha_{s}$, the solar absorptivity, with $\alpha_{\oplus}$ the albedo of the Earth
- $\delta$, the depth of discharge
- $w$, the cell specific energy
- $m_{b}$, the battery mass
- $A_{\text{ref}}$, the drag reference area, while $A$ is the solar array area
- $B$, the ballistic coefficient
- $a_{D}$, the drag deceleration
- $I_{sp}$, the specific impulse in seconds
- $\dot{q}_{s}$, the stagnation-point heat flux
- $R_{n}$, the nose radius
- $\phi$, the bank angle
- $\psi$, the heading angle
- $h_{E}$, the energy height
- $\Phi$, the duty cycle
- $e$, the eccentricity
- $r_{p}$, the perigee radius, with $r_{a}$ the apogee radius
- $v_{p}$, the perigee speed
- $\Delta v_{\text{pass}}$, the velocity removed per perigee pass
